name: The Order of the Trumps
description: Who put the twenty-two trumps in their order, and what the order meant. The pictures came first and the numbers later; three Italian cities ranked them three ways; a preacher wrote the first list down; in 1781 French writers turned it upside down and gave it Hebrew letters; the Golden Dawn moved Strength and Justice to make the zodiac run in order. What the record shows, and what is a reading.

sections.Content:
*Who thought of that order, and what did it mean?* I asked that question for years with an answer already in hand: the sequence was a revelation, a book of Hermes Trismegistus hidden in a card game. Then I learned it wasn't. The order was set by card players in a few Italian cities in the fifteenth century, and they did not agree with one another. Its meaning was a rank in a game first. The stories about a path of the soul came later, and some of them read the cards in the opposite direction.

*Citations use the keys in this library's [bibliography](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/bibliography.bib), as `[@key, p. N]`; the list at the end says what each key is. Short quotations only. "A reading" marks an interpretation, never a fact.*

The oldest trumps carry neither numbers nor names. The hand-painted Milanese cards of the 1440s to 1460s, the Visconti and Visconti-Sforza packs, show their figures with no number and no title [@farley2009, p. 7; @web_vs_wp]. The order was something players held in their heads.

They needed it. These cards were made for a trick-taking game, and a trump wins because it outranks another trump. Helen Farley puts the point simply: the order mattered during a game, and as long as everyone at the table agreed on it, the absolute order mattered much less [@farley2009, p. 44]. The Italian name says the same thing. The cards were *trionfi*, triumphs, and in English that word became *trump*.

An even earlier ranked set shows the habit. Around 1418–1425 Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan had a pack painted with sixteen classical gods, described in a treatise by Marziano da Tortona, a scholar at his court, and the gods were ranked: Jupiter highest, Cupid lowest [@pratesi1989; @web_trionfi_cards_wp]. That pack is lost, and it was not yet the tarot. It shows that a court game of ranked pictures existed before the twenty-two we know.

So the first answer to *who thought of the order* is: nobody we can name. No document records a designer. What survives is a set of local customs, and they differ.

Michael Dummett, the philosopher who rebuilt the history of tarot as a game, sorted the early Italian evidence into three families of trump order. He called them A, B and C. A belongs to Florence and Bologna, B to Ferrara, C to Milan. They differ mainly in two places: the order of the highest trumps, and whether the three virtues sit together or apart [@dummett1980; @ipcs_ps001]. Summarising Dummett's chapter on the regional orders, Wikipedia gives the top of each: in Bologna and Florence the Angel is highest, with the World below it; in Ferrara the World is highest, with Justice and then the Angel beneath; in Milan the World is highest, with the Angel beneath [@web_trionfi_cards_wp; @dummett1980, pp. 387–417].

The Milanese order is the one most people know, because it travelled. Milan fell to French and Swiss armies in the sixteenth century, and the game went north with them. The French and Swiss cardmakers' pattern we now call the Tarot de Marseille kept Milan's order [@farley2009, p. 93; @ipcs_ps001]. The Ferrarese order spread east to Venice and Trento; the Bolognese one south, and to the Savoyard states [@web_trionfi_cards_wp].

Five cards show the differences most clearly:

| Card | A · Bologna | B · Ferrara (the Steele list) | C · Milan, then Marseille | Rider-Waite-Smith, 1909 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperance | 7, first of three virtues side by side | 6, below Love | XIV | XIV |
| Justice | 8, middle of the three | 20, between the Angel and the World | VIII | XI |
| Strength | 9, last of the three | 9 | XI | VIII |
| Wheel of Fortune | 10 | 10 | X | X |
| Angel / Judgement | highest card, unnumbered | 19 | XX | XX |
| World | just below the Angel, unnumbered | 21, highest | XXI, highest | XXI |

*Bologna prints numbers only on trumps 5 to 16; its four "Moors" (once the Popess, Empress, Emperor and Pope) count as equals below Love [@web_tarocco_bolognese_wp]. The Ferrara column uses the list in the next lesson. Marseille numbers from [@ipcs_ps001]; the Rider-Waite-Smith numbers from the cards.*

Look at Justice. In Milan she sits in the lower half, eighth. In Bologna she is one of a cluster of three virtues just above the Chariot. In Ferrara she climbs almost to the top, above the Angel of the Last Judgement and below only the World. The same picture held three different ranks, a few days' ride apart.

nodes.name: The first written list: a sermon against the game

sections.Content:
The earliest surviving list of the trumps in order was written by someone who disliked them. It sits in an anonymous Latin sermon against gambling, in a volume of sermons the antiquarian Robert Steele owned and published in 1900. Steele dated the volume to about 1450–1470 and later, more cautiously, to 1450–1480 [@steele1900, pp. 185–200]; Wikipedia captions the page "Venice, c. 1480–1500" [@web_trionfi_cards_wp]. The dating is still open.

The preacher names twenty-one triumphs, lowest first, and adds the Fool, who counts as nothing: the Bagatella, Empress, Emperor, Popess, Pope, Temperance, Love, the Triumphal Chariot, Fortitude, the Wheel, the Hunchback (the old man of Time), the Hanged Man, Death, the Devil, the Arrow (the card later called the Tower), the Star, the Moon, the Sun, the Angel, Justice, the World [@steele1900, pp. 185–200; @farley2009, p. 84]. Justice between the Angel and the World is the Ferrara pattern.

He also tells us what the order meant to him. He objects that God, the angels, the planets and the cardinal virtues are put into a game, along with the Pope and the Emperor. And he reads the sequence as a ladder, going down. The twenty-one points of a die, he says, are the steps of one ladder into hell; the twenty-one triumphs are "21 gradus alterius scale in profundum inferi mittentis", the steps of another, sending the player into its depths [@steele1900, pp. 185–200]. The first person to write the order down saw a descent, and he meant it as a warning.

Two other kinds of evidence fill out the picture without settling it. The Rosenwald sheets in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, uncut woodcut sheets from Florence of about 1500, show trumps as they were printed for ordinary players; they are pictures, not a list, and they do not complete a pack [@nga_rosenwald; @web_th_rosenwald].

nodes.name: What the order may have meant

sections.Content:
Here the record ends and readings begin. Each of the readings below has a scholar behind it, and each one fits some cards better than others.

**A procession of triumphs.** Petrarch's poem *I Trionfi*, written between 1340 and 1374, is a parade in which each figure overcomes the one before: Love, then Chastity, Death, Fame, Time and Eternity. Petrarch spent years at the Visconti court, and his work was in the Visconti library [@farley2009, p. 45]. The librarian Gertrude Moakley argued, in an article of 1956 and a book of 1966, that the game of triumphs pictured this sequence, as floats in a carnival procession [@moakley1956; @moakley1966; @farley2009, p. 45]. Farley finds the fit hard to make. In paintings of Petrarch's Triumphs every figure rides a car, while only one trump, the Chariot, does; the Duke who commissioned the first packs disliked crowds and spectacle; and there are far more trumps than triumphs, with no obvious place for the Hanged Man or the Popess [@farley2009, pp. 45–46]. What survives of the idea is the logic of *beating*: each card overcoming the one below, the way each Triumph conquers the last.

**A moral ladder.** Read from the bottom, the sequence passes through ranks people knew: the street conjuror, the powers of church and empire, love and the virtues, Fortune's wheel, old age, the hanged traitor, Death, the Devil, the falling tower, the lights of heaven, and the Last Judgement with the World above it. It is easy to see a climb from worldly rank to last things. Fifteenth-century Italy had a ladder of exactly this kind in another set of pictures: the so-called "Mantegna Tarocchi" of about 1465, fifty numbered engravings that rise from a beggar to the First Cause. That set was made as a ladder of being, and it is a cousin of the tarot, not an ancestor [@web_mantegna_wopc]. The early trumps carried no numbers at all, which is one reason to hold the ladder reading lightly. And the preacher who wrote the first list read the same ladder going down.

**A court's own story.** Farley's reading is that the Milanese trumps told the story of the Visconti house through the ideas of its time: death and the hope of eternal life, the Church and the Empire and their corruption, and family figures, Francesco Sforza on the Strength card and Sister Maifreda on the Popess [@farley2009, p. 93]. She also reads the run of Star, Moon and Sun astrologically, from lesser lights to the greatest [@farley2009, p. 78].

**A rank in a game.** Underneath every reading is the fact that the order did its job at the card table, and that it differed from city to city. Farley uses that variation as an argument against the idea that the trumps encoded a fixed system of knowledge: a key that changes by region is a poor key [@farley2009, p. 44].

What is known: the trumps were game cards; they were ranked; the ranking varied by city; the earliest written list is a preacher's. What is a reading: everything about what the sequence was *for* beyond the game. A reading can still be good to live with. It is just not a document.

For three centuries the order belonged to players. In 1781 it gained a meaning from outside the game. In the eighth volume of *Le Monde primitif*, the Protestant scholar Antoine Court de Gébelin claimed the tarot was an ancient Egyptian book: as their libraries burned, Egyptian priests had hidden their knowledge in a game [@farley2009, p. 103]. He tied the twenty-two trumps to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet [@farley2009, p. 104].

His volume carried a second essay, by the Comte de Mellet, a court noble and soldier. Mellet agreed that the cards were Egyptian and that the sequence should be read from the highest number to the lowest [@farley2009, p. 104]. In his scheme the first letter, Aleph, went to the World, trump XXI [@farley2009, p. 106]. He split the trumps into three groups of seven, ages of humankind: XXI to XV the Golden Age, starting with creation; XIV to VIII the Silver Age; VII down to I the Iron Age, ending with the Mountebank who fools the crowd [@farley2009, pp. 104–105]. Read Mellet's way, the trumps are a fall from paradise. Farley notes how close this runs to the ancient Ages of Man and to the Hindu cycle of yugas, both popular in the France of his day [@farley2009, p. 105]. Mellet's essay is also the oldest known text to read tarot for divination [@farley2009, p. 106].

So in the space of one book, the order lost its game and gained a direction. And Mellet's direction is the same as the preacher's: down.

Seventy-five years later Éliphas Lévi turned it the right way up. In *Dogme et rituel de la haute magie* (1856) he kept the Marseille order, gave Aleph to trump I, the Magician, and put the unnumbered Fool near the end, between Judgement (XX) and the World (XXI), with the letter Shin [@levi1856; @farley2009, p. 113]. Farley points to the weak spot in all of this: the French writers worked from the Marseille pattern alone and had no idea that other orders existed, though their theories depended on the order [@farley2009, p. 120].

nodes.name: The Golden Dawn's swap: Strength and Justice

sections.Content:
The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in London in 1888, built its tarot on the Cipher Manuscript, a coded document of uncertain authorship. It took the Fool from the end of Lévi's list and put it first, so the Fool became Aleph and every trump moved one letter along [@farley2009, pp. 132–133].

That move broke something, and the zodiac shows where. In the *Sefer Yetzirah*, the old Hebrew book the Order followed, twelve of the letters belong to the twelve signs, in order. With the Fool as Aleph, the Marseille numbers land like this [@equinox1912_bookt, pp. 150–151]:

| Trump (Marseille number) | Letter, with the Fool as Aleph | Sign of that letter |
|---|---|---|
| IV Emperor | He | Aries |
| V Pope | Vav | Taurus |
| VI Lovers | Zayin | Gemini |
| VII Chariot | Cheth | Cancer |
| **VIII Justice** | **Teth** | **Leo** |
| IX Hermit | Yod | Virgo |
| X Wheel | Kaph | Jupiter (a planet, not a sign) |
| **XI Strength** | **Lamed** | **Libra** |

The woman with the scales lands on the lion's sign, and the woman with the lion lands on the sign of the scales. Exchange the two and each picture meets its own sign: Strength with Leo and Teth, Justice with Libra and Lamed, and the signs run Aries to Libra in order. That is the reason the historians give for the swap: a better astrological fit [@farley2009, pp. 133, 139]. I did not find the Order explaining it in its own words; the reason is visible in the arithmetic.

What exactly was swapped needs care. In *Book T*, the Order's tarot text, as printed in *The Equinox* in 1912, Fortitude stands eighth in the list, between the Chariot and the Hermit, on Teth and Leo; Justice stands eleventh, on Lamed and Libra. But the printed numbers stay the old ones: Fortitude is still 11 and Justice still 8 [@equinox1912_bookt, pp. 150–151]. The Order moved the attributions. The first printed cards to carry the new numbers, Strength VIII and Justice XI, are the Rider-Waite-Smith deck of 1909. A. E. Waite's book takes the change on himself, "for reasons which satisfy myself", and declines to explain [@waite1910]. Farley says Mathers renumbered the two cards in the pattern deck members copied [@farley2009, p. 135]; that deck is lost, and this library has not traced the claim to a document. A longer note on what each source prints is in [the Strength and Justice note](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/synthesis/strength-justice-numbering.md).

Aleister Crowley, who had been a member, kept the old numbers and the new letters in his Thoth deck: VIII Adjustment (Justice) on Libra, XI Lust (Strength) on Leo [@farley2009, p. 140; @web_thoth_tarot_wp]. Seen as a line through the zodiac, the Leo–Libra exchange makes a small loop. Crowley added a second exchange at the other end, on the strength of a line in his *Book of the Law*: the letter Tzaddi went from the Star to the Emperor, and He from the Emperor to the Star, so Aries and Aquarius trade places around Pisces. His own image was two matching loops at the two ends of an ellipse [@farley2009, pp. 139–140; @web_thoth_tarot_wp].

So the Golden Dawn did not reveal a hidden order. It inherited Milan's order by way of Marseille and Lévi, changed where it began, and then repaired the zodiac in one place.

Where did the Hermes story come from? From the same French circle. Court de Gébelin's Egyptian book of 1781 became, in Etteilla's hands a few years later, a book designed by seventeen magi under Hermes Trismegistus, 171 years after the Flood [@farley2009, p. 107]. Etteilla reasoned that if the tarot was the Book of Thoth, and Thoth was Hermes Trismegistus, then Hermetic wisdom must be in the cards [@farley2009, p. 109]. Papus in 1889 called the tarot "the book of Thoth Hermes Trismegistus" [@farley2009, p. 118]. The Golden Dawn's Cipher Manuscript calls the trumps the mansions of Thoth [@farley2009, p. 132], and Crowley called his book *The Book of Thoth*. By the twentieth century the idea was in most occult tarot books, and that is likely where many of us met it.

The Hermetic writings themselves are real: Greek texts by writers who believed Egypt held a pure ancient philosophy and its magic. Renaissance readers took them for works of ancient Egypt. In 1614 the scholar Isaac Casaubon cast doubt on that; Protestant Europe largely accepted his case, while in Catholic France the enthusiasm went on [@farley2009, p. 104]. The French tarot writers worked before anyone could read hieroglyphs, inside a fashion for all things Egyptian [@farley2009, p. 104]. Farley calls the Egyptian story a myth its own makers never convincingly verified [@farley2011, p. 175].

Could there have been an older, hidden source behind the fifteenth-century cards? The record cannot rule out every possibility. Nothing found so far points there. The earliest trumps come from Italian courts and print shops; their order changed from city to city; the people who first claimed a revelation did not know the other orders existed; and the writers who first gave the sequence a cosmic meaning did not agree which way it ran. The odds favour people, cities and card tables.

That does not empty the order of meaning. It moves the meaning to us. A sequence made by players, read as a descent by a preacher, as a fall by Mellet, as a climb by Lévi, and as a map of the zodiac by the Golden Dawn has been, for nearly six centuries, a place where people put what they believed about the world. Reading it as a path today is one more turn of that. The difference is that we can sign our reading. Which direction do you read it in, and why?

The keys used above, all in [`research/bibliography.bib`](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/bibliography.bib):

- `dummett1980`: Michael Dummett, *The Game of Tarot: From Ferrara to Salt Lake City* (London: Duckworth, 1980). The A, B, C orders. Not read directly for this course: the page range for the regional orders (pp. 387–417) is the one Wikipedia gives, and the summary of the orders comes through `web_trionfi_cards_wp` and `ipcs_ps001`.
- `farley2009`: Helen Farley, *A Cultural History of Tarot: From Entertainment to Esotericism* (London: I.B. Tauris, 2009). Read in a library copy; page numbers are that edition's.
- `farley2011`: Helen Farley, "Out of Africa: Tarot's Fascination With Egypt," *Literature & Aesthetics* 21:1 (2011). [Open access](https://openjournals.library.sydney.edu.au/index.php/LA/article/view/5055).
- `steele1900`: Robert Steele, "A Notice of the Ludus Triumphorum and Some Early Italian Card Games," *Archaeologia* 57 (1900), pp. 185–200. The sermon's Latin, [transcribed at tarock.info](https://www.tarock.info/steele.htm).
- `moakley1956` and `moakley1966`: Gertrude Moakley, "The Tarot Trumps and Petrarch's *Trionfi*" (*Bulletin of the New York Public Library*, 1956) and *The Tarot Cards Painted by Bonifacio Bembo* (1966). Cited for her thesis; Farley's critique is cited from Farley.
- `pratesi1989`: Franco Pratesi, "The Earliest Tarot Pack Known" (1989), [naibi.net](https://www.naibi.net/A/25-FIRSTARO-Z.pdf).
- `levi1856`: Éliphas Lévi, *Dogme et rituel de la haute magie* (Paris, 1856).
- `equinox1912_bookt`: *Book T*, in *The Equinox* I(8) (London, 1912), pp. 143–210, public domain. [Scan](https://archive.org/details/IAPSOP-equinox_v1_n8_1912_Sep); the whole text is [on this site](book-t.html).
- `waite1910`: A. E. Waite, *The Pictorial Key to the Tarot* (London: Rider, 1910; dated 1911 in many editions), under "Strength".
- `ipcs_ps001`: International Playing-Card Society, [Pattern Sheet 001, Tarot de Marseille Type I](https://i-p-c-s.org/pattern/PS001.pdf) (2018).
- `web_trionfi_cards_wp`: Wikipedia, ["Trionfi (cards)"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trionfi_(cards)), read 13 October 2026.
- `web_tarocco_bolognese_wp`: Wikipedia, ["Tarocco Bolognese"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarocco_Bolognese).
- `web_thoth_tarot_wp`: Wikipedia, ["Thoth Tarot"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoth_Tarot), read 13 October 2026, for Crowley's own wording.
- `web_vs_wp`, `web_mantegna_wopc`, `nga_rosenwald`, `web_th_rosenwald`: the Visconti-Sforza, Mantegna and Rosenwald dossiers' sources, in this library's [research folder](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/tree/main/research).

Related reading here: [The History of Tarot](course-viewer.html?course=history-of-tarot), [The Golden Dawn — the Map and the Walk](course-viewer.html?course=walking-the-golden-dawn-path), and [Same Card, Every Deck](course-viewer.html?course=same-card-every-deck).
